briefing.opening: Good day. We begin the Climate Briefing for November 13, 2026.

sections.title: 🌍 Opening of the COP31 Summit and Desperate Appeals from Climate-Vulnerable Nations
sections.content: As the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) World Leaders Summit got underway, leaders of nations severely battered by climate change strongly urged immediate and urgent action from the international community [71, 73, 77, 85]. Attending a UN climate summit for the first time in five years, Swedish environmental activist Greta Thunberg warned that the Earth is not dying but being murdered, criticizing world leaders' complacency [55, 97]. However, as negotiations began in earnest, concerns mounted that conflicting priorities among global leaders are putting existing climate targets further out of reach, prompting criticism that the conference is turning into a mere diplomatic showcase [79, 88, 90]. Meanwhile, South Korea's Presidential Special Envoy Kang Geum-sil delivered an address at the summit, emphasizing international solidarity in tackling the climate crisis [1, 8, 16].

sections.title: ⚠️ Accelerating Climate Disasters and Deepening Global Crisis
sections.content: Assessments indicate that while global average temperatures continue to climb, global climate action remains largely at a standstill [4, 70]. Scientists warned that the combined impacts of climate change and the El Niño phenomenon have severely worsened wildfire destruction and meteorological hazards across Indonesia's peatlands and forests [57, 63, 68, 91]. Furthermore, climate change is inflicting multifaceted social and environmental damage, melting polar and mountain ice and exerting a disproportionately severe impact on women's health [56, 60, 78]. Amid this crisis, the UK government has faced criticism for deciding not to release a crucial report that warned of national security risks posed by global ecosystem collapse [96].

sections.title: 🇰🇷 South Korea's Bottom-Tier Climate Action Rating and Energy Infrastructure Challenges
sections.content: South Korea has ranked near the very bottom at 61st in climate action assessments, weighed down by sluggish greenhouse gas reductions and lagging energy transition [18]. In particular, as prospects for achieving the government's 100 GW renewable energy target grow uncertain, policy alerts are heightening—marked by the unveiling of a '100 GW Renewable Energy Traffic Light' system to monitor implementation progress [39, 40]. In response, the Korea Power Exchange has decided to mobilize all capabilities within its power grid control tower to prepare for the surge in AI and renewable energy [42]. In addition, the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) highlighted environmental disclosure loopholes among Big Tech firms driven by the proliferation of AI data centers, calling for the establishment of carbon emission disclosure standards [14].

sections.title: 🌱 Agricultural R&D and Technological Solutions for Climate Adaptation
sections.content: As climate change threatens agricultural water security and food supply stability, agricultural adaptation research is actively advancing both domestically and abroad [2, 5, 15]. In South Korea, developing new domestic rice varieties capable of withstanding climate change and extreme heat was highlighted as an urgent priority, while South Korea and Japan agreed to expand bilateral R&D cooperation in agriculture, forestry, and fisheries [9, 11, 13, 17]. Diverse countermeasures are also being explored in the technology sector, such as carbon removal research combining crushed rock with AI models, and the publication of a technical white paper on grid-forming ESS to support power grid stability [46, 62]. Internationally, field-level adaptation efforts continue, including nature-friendly tea cultivation adaptation in Taiwan and research to protect cocoa crops used for chocolate production [72, 83].

sections.title: 🌱 Local Governments and Civil Society Spearhead Carbon Neutrality Practices
sections.content: Community- and public agency-led models of carbon neutrality practices—directly experienced and joined by residents—are expanding [21, 27]. Nowon-gu in Seoul was designated an 'Environmental Education City 2026' by the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment and will strengthen practical education for three years, while Gwanak-gu is rolling out a resident-participatory green living certification campaign [22, 23, 24, 30]. In the financial sector, KB Kookmin Bank and Industrial Bank of Korea (IBK) are offering bonus Carbon Neutral Points to customers registered as climate citizens on their mobile apps, incentivizing everyday carbon-cutting actions [35]. Alongside these efforts, basic local governments are actively establishing tangible infrastructure, such as Uijeongbu City's creation of a carbon neutrality demonstration garden [31].

briefing.closing: As signals of the global climate crisis become increasingly pronounced, the tangible implementation of international cooperation and proactive, community-driven mitigation efforts are more critical than ever. This concludes today's Climate Briefing.
